newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn denies 1997 deficit to reach 3.5 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Bonn denies 1997 deficit to reach 3.5 pct of GDP.

text.p: The Finance Ministry on Wednesday denied a German newspaper report that Germany's 1997 public sector deficit would exceed the limit for participating in the European monetary union.

A Finance Ministry spokesman said the Berliner Zeitung report that the deficit would reach 3.5 percent of gross domestic product was not in line with ministry projections, which still see a deficit of 2.9 percent.
"For us, the figure remains 2.9 percent," the spokesman said, noting that state secretary Juergen Stark had confirmed that figure late on Wednesday and said it already reflected all recognised risks.
The Maastricht Treaty says countries hoping to participate in EMU at the 1999 start must keep their 1997 deficits below three percent of GDP.

The Berlin daily, citing Chancellor Helmut Kohl's office and coalition sources, reported that some Bonn budget experts thought 20 billion marks in additional spending cuts were needed this year for Germany to meet the goal.
Chancellery officials were not immediately available for comment.
The coalition discussed further spending cuts on Tuesday, particularly in social spending, but the 20 billion mark figure did not come up, a participant in the talks told Reuters.
Another government source, however, said the cuts could reach that size.
The newspaper said Finance Minister Theo Waigel would make a decision about a spending freeze "very soon".
Waigel has said bills already passed by the lower house of parliament and now before the mediation committee would cut spending by five billion marks.
